newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgium faces week of drama in minister sex probe.
newsitem.headline: Belgium faces week of drama in minister sex probe.

text.p: Belgium faces another week of political drama as its highest court investigates child sex allegations against Deputy Prime Minister Elio di Rupo with the opposition renewing calls for his resignation.

"Di Rupo must resign. The man cannot function as a minister. He is subject of a judicial investigation. How can he be member of a government that is about to reform the justice system," Pierre Chevalier, parliament member for the opposition Flemish liberal party VLD, said on BRTN television on Sunday.

Parliament last Thursday asked the Cour de Cassation to investigate allegations made in a report by the Brussels prosecutor general that Di Rupo, 45, had had sex with under-age boys at parties in 1989-90.
The legal age of consent in Belgium is 16, both for heterosexual and homosexual relations. Di Rupo, a discreet homosexual, has denied the allegations.
The Cour, Belgium's highest court, must make a new report to parliament by December 9.
Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene has so far backed his deputy has lashed out at the prosecutor for basing his case against Di Rupo on flimsy evidence.
Tony Van Parys, a parliament member of Dehaene's Christian- Democrat CVP party, expressed renewed support for Di Rupo.

"I can accept that in this period (until December 9) Di Rupo remains somewhat in the background, but I cannot accept that he should be forced to resign based on such unverified rumours," he said in a BRTN television debate on Sunday.

Several newspapers said on Friday that the sole witness who alleged Di Rupo had sex with under-age boys was not credible and suggested the judiciary had attacked Di Rupo to deflect the government from reforming the justice system.

That system has been widely criticised for its handling of a child murder scandal centring around Marc Dutroux, the main suspect in a paedophile ring which has claimed the lives of at least four girls.
The centre-left coalition government is preparing a review of the justice system, against the background of the three-month-old murder scandal.
Separately, a parliamentary commission is also investigating accusations by the families of the victims that the police and justice systems made mistakes in the Dutroux investigation.

On Sunday, Serge Moureaux, a member of the parliament's Dutroux commission, joined several other political commentators who have said that the justice and police system are trying to discredit politicians in order to block the long-delayed reforms of the courts and the police forces.

Moureaux, who belongs to Di Rupo's socialist party PS, told RTBF radio that he had proof that members of the Belgian police were probing the private life of members of the Dutroux commission in order to intimidate them.
"I want to warn all those who have thought up this kind of enquiry against their own foolishness...and I hope the commission members will keep their cool and not become paranoid," Moureaux said.
The commission is meeting Sunday afternoon for discussions with the parents of missing children.

Analysts have said that if the Cour de Cassation clears Di Rupo's name, political debate in Belgium will be forced to focus on whether it is acceptable that the number two in the Belgian government is a homosexual.

Catholic daily De Standaard, which first leaked the allegations against Di Rupo last weekend, on Friday questioned whether Di Rupo's lifestyle was fit for someone "who must represent his country and the King".
